newsitem.title: ROMANIA: FOCUS - Romania eyes solid export-led growth to 2000.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Romania eyes solid export-led growth to 2000.

text.p: Romania, faced with an ailing economy, outlined on Monday its development targets before the turn of the century, pledging to achieve solid, export-driven economic growth.

"The main goal of (our) macro-economic policy is to attain a strong and durable growth, which, in the long term, would lead to a rise in living standards and narrow the economic gap between Romania and the European Union," said a document worked out by the government's Economic Reform Council.
It forecast a reversal of this year's 3.0 percent fall in gross domestic product (GDP), saying a gradual uptrend was expected in 1998, when GDP was seen growing by 2.3 percent.
A 4.0 percent GDP growth rate, close to last year's 4.1 percent, is expected by the year 2000, when 12-month inflation is seen at 15 percent, sharply down from 97 percent this year.

In a first stage, economic policy will focus on macro- economic stability, working to fight inflation, strengthening financial discipline and slashing the budget and current account deficits, the document said.
Romania's centrist coalition government, which ousted leftists in last November's elections, promised a shock-therapy programme to reshape the economy by accelerating privatisation and restructuring.
It has already tightened monetary and budgetary policies and freed the foreign exchange market and energy and food prices.

Price liberalisation pushed inflation to a monthly rate of 30.7 percent in March before slowing to 6.9 in April. The cabinet aims to cut inflation to a monthly two percent or so by end-1997, in line with accords with international lenders.

"Commercial policy will have a crucial role in underpinning solid growth...Exports will become a leverage to dynamise the economy," said the document, which estimates a 2.5 percent rise in exports this year after a 3.2 percent fall in 1996.
Higher export growth rates of 5.0 percent are seen by 2000.
The document also said deep reforms to cut losses in farming and large energy-consuming sectors would consolidate economic stability and bring much-needed foreign inflows.

"The attainment of our targets by stepping up structural reforms will help the economy to adapt to the macro-economic demands imposed by long-term high-rate economic growth, all while furthering anti-inflationary policy," it said.
The private sector is expected to take 80 percent of GDP in 2000, sharply up from 52 percent last year.

"By 2000, there should be not only a durable growth but also retreating unemployment...We estimate faster privatisation and restructuring will cut unemployment to 8.7 percent by 2000," the document said.
The jobless rate is seen soaring to 10.3 percent this year from 6.1 percent at end-1996 as Romania advances with plans to restructure its communist-era industries.
